note: Higashiyama's daily life (issue #357): the people to know, their hours, the jobs, the counters and the calendar. Built into web/data/higashiyama/life.json by pipeline/life.py, which resolves every place. Facts in 'fact' are checked against the sources in docs/cities/higashiyama.md and docs/cities/kyoto-sights.md; each event carries its own source. Higashiyama Hanatouro is not listed: it has not been held since March 2022.

bonds.title: The kimono shop
bonds.busy: I've three customers and one obi between them. Come in the daytime, or at dusk when the returns are in.

ranks.title: Forty-six metres
ranks.invite: You've stopped where everyone stops. Have you a little of the {slot}? I'll tell you what you're actually looking at.
talk: The pagoda belongs to a temple called Hokan-ji, and the pagoda is nearly all that's left of it. Forty-six metres. This one went up in 1440, when a shogun paid for it.
It's one of the few you can go inside, on the days they open it. You climb a ladder to the second storey and look down at us through a little window.
ranks.fact: The Yasaka Pagoda of Hokan-ji is 46 m tall and was rebuilt in 1440 with the support of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshinori.

ask.q: Where do you think the photograph is taken from?

options.reply: Just here, where the roofs frame it. You'll see forty people doing it at four o'clock.
Too close: you get a wall. Come down the street and let the roofs frame it.

request.text: Photograph the pagoda from Yasaka-dori (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Go on, take it. From the street, looking up. Photo mode, then show me.

ranks.title: The bound monkeys
talk: That's the one. You didn't even cut off the top.
Now the colours next door, at Koshin-do. Those cloth balls are monkeys, kukurizaru, with their hands and feet tied together. A monkey that can't run after what it wants.
You write a wish on one and give up one craving in exchange. My customers give up sweets. For about a day.
ranks.fact: The coloured balls at Yasaka Koshin-do are kukurizaru, monkeys with bound hands and feet: a wish is written on one in exchange for giving up one desire.

request.text: Try something from a counter on the lanes
request.ask: Have you eaten? There's yatsuhashi on Ninenzaka. Go on, I'll still be here.

ranks.title: A bag for the gate
talk: Cinnamon on your breath. Good, you've given up nothing.
Here's a thing that pays. A customer has gone up to the temple in my kimono and left her own bag on my counter. Take it up to the red gate before she notices and panics.
ranks.fact: Kiyomizu-dera's Deva Gate, the Niomon, stands about 14 m high and was rebuilt around 1500 after the fires of the Onin War.

gives.name: Aiko's runner
gives.text: A paid delivery from the shop, in your diary under Work

request.text: Take the customer's bag up to the Deva Gate
request.ask: The bag's on the counter, the pink one. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: Lantern hour
talk: She got her bag. She cried a little. They always do.
Stay till the lamps come on. These lanes have no poles and no wires overhead: the city buried them, so at dusk there's only roofs, lanterns and the pagoda.
Here, let me set your camera for it. Warm, a little soft, the way it looks to someone walking home.
ranks.fact: The overhead wires along Yasaka-dori, Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka have been buried, leaving the lanes free of utility poles.

gives.name: Lantern light
gives.text: Photographs after sunset come out warm, as the lanes look by lantern

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Bring me one picture from the good hour, when the lanterns and the sky are the same brightness.

ranks.title: Okoshiyasu
talk: That's my street. You made it look the way I see it going home.
You know what the Kyoto girls say when they laugh at my customers? Nothing. They say 'how nice, you look so comfortable.' That's the laugh.
You, I'll tell straight: come back. おこしやす means that, more or less.
ranks.fact: Okoshiyasu is the Kyoto dialect's welcome, a warmer and more formal form of oideyasu.

gives.name: Aiko's regulars
gives.text: 20% more for every job in Higashiyama

bonds.title: The potter on Sannenzaka
bonds.busy: The shop's full, forgive me. Come when it rains: the lane empties, and I can sit at the wheel and talk.

ranks.title: Tea-bowl slope
ranks.invite: Rain. Good. Nobody buys pots in the rain. Have you a little of the {slot}? Sit down, and mind the shelf.
talk: Kiyomizu-yaki was never one style. It's whatever the potters on these slopes made for people going up to the temple: tea bowls, sake cups, incense boxes.
The next lane south is Chawan-zaka, tea-bowl slope, though the signs say Teapot Lane. My grandfather's kiln was at the bottom of it, on Gojo-zaka.
ranks.fact: Kiyomizu-yaki, Kyoto's pottery, grew up from the 1600s on the slopes below Kiyomizu-dera; Chawan-zaka, 'tea-bowl slope', is named for it.

ask.q: What do you think a tea bowl is judged by?

options.text: How it sits in two hands
options.reply: Yes. You close your eyes and hold it. If you forget it's there, it's a good one.
That's for the shelf. Close your eyes and hold it: if you forget it's there, it's good.

request.text: Choose something from Mr. Fujii's shelf
request.ask: Have you picked one up yet? Don't buy the prettiest. Buy the one your hand goes back to.

ranks.title: The cold kilns
talk: That one. I'd have chosen it for you.
We used to fire in climbing kilns: long brick tunnels up the slope of Gojo-zaka, burning pine for two days. The whole hill smoked.
Around 1970 the smoke rules came and the kilns went cold. Most of us moved over the hill to Yamashina. I fire with electricity now, and I miss the pine.
ranks.fact: Gojo-zaka's wood-fired climbing kilns stopped around 1970 under air-pollution rules, and many Kiyomizu-yaki potters moved to a pottery estate in Yamashina.

gives.name: A potter's eye
gives.text: Eye: you see when a line is true

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Go and judge the pagoda by eye. Press G, say a height, and tell me how near you came.

ranks.title: Three years
talk: Close. A potter would have been closer, but close.
The steps outside. They say that if you fall on Sannenzaka you die within three years. So the shop at the bottom sells gourds: a gourd catches the bad luck, you see.
The other story is kinder. 産寧, safe birth: this was the road up to the Koyasu pagoda, where women prayed before a child came.
ranks.fact: Sannenzaka is also written 産寧坂, 'safe-birth slope': it was the approach to Kiyomizu-dera's Koyasu pagoda, where prayers for an easy childbirth are made.

options.reply: So do I. But I sell more cups to people who have just heard the other.
Then hold the rail, and buy a gourd at the bottom.

gives.name: Mr. Fujii's carrier
gives.text: A paid delivery of pots, in your diary under Work

request.text: Carry the crate of cups to the tea house by Yasaka Shrine
request.ask: The crate is packed in straw by the door. It's in your diary, under Work. Walk, don't run.

ranks.title: The work is the signature
talk: Nothing chipped. You carried it as if it were yours.
If you want to see a real climbing kiln, Kawai Kanjiro's house on Gojo-zaka keeps one in the back garden, cold since he died. For the second half of his life he never signed a pot.
He said the work was the signature. I sign mine. I'm not Kawai.
ranks.fact: The potter Kawai Kanjiro (1890-1966), whose house and climbing kiln on Gojo-zaka are now a museum, left his later work unsigned and declined the title of Living National Treasure.

gives.name: A craftsman's word
gives.text: 15% more for every job in Higashiyama

request.ask: Keep judging things by eye. Heights, widths, the lean of a wall. Then come back on a wet day.

ranks.title: The one that warped
talk: You've been looking properly. It shows in how you stand in a doorway.
This bowl warped in the kiln, twenty years ago. I meant to break it. My wife put rice in it instead, and now it's the only one I use.
Take your time over things. The rain will stop when it stops.
ranks.fact: Kyo-yaki and Kiyomizu-yaki, the pottery of Kyoto, were designated one of Japan's traditional crafts in 1977.

gives.name: Two hands
gives.text: Eye, from a man who throws to the millimetre

bonds.title: The monk at the red gate
bonds.busy: I must see to the hall. I am at the gate in the mornings: the temple opens at six, every day of the year.

ranks.title: Six o'clock
ranks.invite: Good morning. You have come before the school trips. If you have a little of the {slot}, walk a few steps with me.
talk: The temple opens at six, every day, and has no closing day. At that hour there are a few neighbours, a few crows, and the sound of the falls.
It was founded in 778, before Kyoto was the capital. The city came to us, not the other way about.
ranks.fact: Kiyomizu-dera opens at 6:00 every day of the year; it was founded in 778, sixteen years before Kyoto became the capital.

ask.q: Why do you suppose it is called the Temple of Pure Water?

options.text: For the falls below the hall
options.reply: Yes. The Otowa spring was here first, and the temple was built beside it. Kiyomizu: clear water.

options.text: For the rain on its roofs
options.reply: A pleasant thought. It is the Otowa spring, below the hall: it was here before we were.

request.ask: Have you been down to the falls? Take one stream only. The guidebooks promise a great deal.

ranks.title: One spring
talk: One stream. Good. Some drink from all three, to be sure of love, long life and their examinations.
It is one spring, divided in three by a carpenter. I should not say so: the queue is good for patience.
ranks.fact: The three streams of the Otowa Falls at Kiyomizu-dera come from a single spring.

gives.name: An early start
gives.text: Bearings: you know the hill before it fills

request.text: Stand on the Stage of Kiyomizu
request.ask: Go out on the stage and look down. Then come and tell me whether you would jump.

ranks.title: To jump from the stage
talk: You looked down. Thirteen metres.
People did jump. The temple's own diaries count 234 between 1694 and 1864, in the belief that Kannon grants the wish of one who survives.
Most lived: about eighty-five in a hundred. The trees were thicker then. It was forbidden in 1872, and I am glad not to keep that diary.
ranks.fact: Temple records count 234 jumps from the stage of Kiyomizu-dera between 1694 and 1864; about 85% survived, and the practice was banned in 1872.

options.reply: Then you understand the saying better than those who use it. 'To jump from the stage of Kiyomizu' means to decide, not to fall.
The saying means to make up one's mind, you know. The stairs also lead down.

request.ask: Walk the precinct a little more. When you can find the falls without the signs, come back.

ranks.title: No nails
talk: You know your way now. So look under the stage as you leave.
Eighteen pillars of zelkova, the tallest about twelve metres, tied by beams that pass straight through them. Not one nail. The wood swells in the rain and holds tighter.
The pillars are four hundred years old. We have planted zelkova in the hills for the next ones. They will be ready in three or four centuries.
ranks.fact: The stage of Kiyomizu-dera stands on 18 zelkova pillars joined by through-beams without nails; the temple has planted zelkova to supply replacement timber centuries from now.

request.text: Stand on the stage in the first hour of the day
request.ask: Come up once at six, before anyone. Stand on the stage and say nothing.

ranks.title: The beam
talk: You came at six. I saw you from the gate, and left you alone.
Three times a year we open at night, and a single blue beam goes up over the city from here. It stands for Kannon's compassion. Children think it is for aeroplanes.
On those nights, wherever you are in Kyoto, you will know which way the hill is.
ranks.fact: During Kiyomizu-dera's night openings in spring, mid-August and autumn, a single blue beam of light is cast into the sky from the temple, standing for Kannon's compassion.

gives.name: The first hour
gives.text: Light, from the hill at six in the morning

bonds.title: The pilgrim with the camera
bonds.busy: Can't talk, the light's going and I haven't got my shot! Find me in the daytime or towards evening.

ranks.title: The same angle
ranks.invite: You look like someone who'd hold a bag. Got a bit of the {slot}? I'll show you where the frame is.
talk: The film came out in 2003. Crossroad in the Ancient Capital, the seventh one. I've seen it nineteen times.
The shot everyone wants is the stage from the Okunoin, across the gully: the whole hall on its pillars with the city behind. It's on every postcard for a reason.
ranks.fact: Detective Conan: Crossroad in the Ancient Capital, the seventh film of the series, came out in 2003 and is set in Kyoto, with Kiyomizu-dera among its scenes.

ask.q: Guess why the Okunoin has a stage too.

options.text: It's built like the main hall, only smaller
options.reply: Right?! Same idea, on stilts over the cliff, just smaller. And it sits right above the falls.
Ha, I wish. It's built like the main hall, on stilts over the cliff, only smaller. Right above the falls.

request.text: Photograph the stage from the Okunoin (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Go round to the Okunoin and take the shot. Photo mode. Then show me, I want to compare.

ranks.title: Autumn
talk: Yes! That's it, that's the frame.
In the manga they come in autumn, on a school trip, and the whole gully under the stage is red. About a thousand maples down there.
I came in the wrong month on purpose. Fewer elbows.
ranks.fact: The gully below Kiyomizu-dera's stage holds about 1,000 maples, at their reddest from mid-November to early December.

gives.name: The frame
gives.text: Light: you see where the picture is

request.ask: Have you done Yasaka Shrine? It's in the school-trip story too. Fifteen minutes north, past Kodai-ji.

ranks.title: The beauty shrine
talk: You went! Did you see the little shrine on the east side, Utsukushi-gozen? Three goddesses of beauty, and a spring in front. You dab the water on your skin.
The maiko from Gion come to it. I dabbed quite a lot.
ranks.fact: Utsukushi-gozen-sha, a small shrine in the grounds of Yasaka Shrine, is dedicated to three goddesses of beauty; visitors dab its spring water on their skin.

ask.q: Did it work, do you think?

options.text: You look exactly the same: good
options.reply: Smooth. Very smooth. OK, you can carry the tripod too.
Wow. OK. Brutal. I'm telling the next goddess about you.

request.ask: There's a list in your diary, under Work: four frames. I need them for my blog. It pays, sort of.

ranks.title: Gojo Bridge
talk: These are better than mine. I'm not even upset.
The fight at the end of the film is on Gojo Ohashi, down the hill, where Benkei met Yoshitsune in the old story. There are statues of the two of them in the middle of the road, round as dumplings.
I stood there for an hour. A bus driver waved.
ranks.fact: By legend the warrior monk Benkei and the young Yoshitsune duelled on Kyoto's Gojo bridge; stone statues of the pair stand in the road at the west end of today's Gojo Ohashi.

gives.name: A credit on the blog
gives.text: 25% more for every job in Higashiyama

request.ask: Shoot a bit more at the ends of the day. When you stop checking the screen after every frame, find me.

ranks.title: One truth
talk: Look at you, not checking the screen. I'm so proud.
I know it's a cartoon. But I planned this trip for two years, and the places were all real, every one, exactly where the drawings said.
真実はいつもひとつ. The truth is I just wanted to come to Kyoto.
ranks.fact: The main hall of Kiyomizu-dera, with its stage, was rebuilt in 1633 and is a National Treasure.

gives.name: A pilgrim's patience
gives.text: Light, from someone who waits for the shot

jobs.title: Which way from Ninenzaka?
jobs.blurb: Visitors at the foot of Ninenzaka ask the way. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.done: They bow, and shuffle off in the right direction.

jobs.title: The pilgrim's four frames
jobs.blurb: Mika's blog wants the pagoda, the Deva Gate, the stage and the falls. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: Mika posts them before you've put the camera away.

jobs.title: A bag for the Deva Gate
jobs.blurb: From Aiko's shop on Yasaka-dori up through the lanes to a customer waiting at Kiyomizu-dera's red gate.
jobs.text: One pink handbag, heavier than it looks. Uphill all the way, and mind the steps.
jobs.done: "My phone was in there!" She bows to the bag.

jobs.title: Cups for the tea house
jobs.blurb: A crate of Mr. Fujii's cups, from Sannenzaka down the lanes to a tea house by Yasaka Shrine's south gate.
jobs.to_name: the tea house by Yasaka Shrine
jobs.text: Twelve tea cups packed in straw. They ring against each other if you hurry.

shops.name: Yatsuhashi counter 八ツ橋
shops.hello: おこしやす. Taste one first: cinnamon, or matcha?

menu.name: Nama yatsuhashi
menu.text: A soft triangle of rice dough scented with cinnamon, folded over red bean. The baked kind is older: a hard biscuit curved like a koto.

menu.name: Warabi mochi
menu.text: Cold, trembling squares rolled in roasted soybean flour. They should give up without a fight, and be gone in a minute.

shops.name: Mr. Fujii's shelf 清水焼
shops.hello: Pick them up. They're for hands, not eyes.

menu.name: A Kiyomizu-yaki cup
menu.text: Thin, pale blue, with one brushed line that doesn't quite meet itself. It warms in the hand before the tea does.

menu.name: A chopstick rest
menu.text: A small glazed aubergine to rest your chopsticks on. The potter's apprentices make these first, by the hundred, until the hands know.

shops.name: Tea house by the falls 茶屋
shops.hello: Sit, sit. You've climbed far enough.

menu.name: Amazake
menu.text: Sweet, cloudy and warm, made from rice and koji, with a pinch of ginger on top. Pilgrims' fuel since long before vending machines.

menu.name: Yudofu
menu.text: Tofu warmed in a pot of kombu broth and lifted out with a little net. Kyoto's water is soft, which is why its tofu is.

events.title: Kiyomizu-dera by night: spring
events.native: 清水寺 春の夜間特別拝観
events.verb: Go in through the lit gate
events.text: In most years the temple stays open until 21:30 for about ten days from late March, with its cherries lit and a blue beam over the city.
lines: The red gate is lit from below, and the cherries beside the three-storey pagoda are white against the dark. The temple is open until half past nine.
From behind the main hall a single blue beam goes up over the city: Kannon's compassion, the temple says. In 2026 the spring evenings ran from 27 March to 5 April.

events.title: Sennichi-mairi: a thousand days in one
events.verb: Climb to the hall by lantern light
events.text: A visit to Kannon on these days of August is said to earn the merit of a thousand. On 14 to 16 August the temple opens at night for it.
lines: One visit on these days counts as a thousand, they say: three years of mornings saved in an evening. The hall is open until half past nine, and its inner sanctuary too.
On the 16th the bonfires burn on the mountains round the city to see the ancestors off. Then the lanterns here feel like part of the same thing.

events.title: Kiyomizu-dera by night: autumn
events.native: 清水寺 秋の夜間特別拝観
events.verb: Go in to see the lit maples
events.text: From the second half of November in most years the temple opens until 21:30, with the maples under the stage lit from below.
lines: The queue runs back down Kiyomizu-zaka. Inside, about a thousand maples in the gully under the stage are lit from below, red on black.
The stage seems to float on them. In 2026 the autumn evenings run from 21 to 30 November.

events.title: Setsubun at Yasaka Shrine
events.verb: Join the crowd at the dance stage
events.text: On 2 and 3 February, maiko and geiko of Kyoto's entertainment districts dance on the shrine's stage and then throw lucky beans to the crowd.
lines: On the dance stage, maiko in long sleeves dance one short piece. Then they pick up wooden boxes and throw paper packets of roasted beans into several hundred lifted hands.
Out with the demons, in with good luck: it is the eve of spring by the old calendar. You eat one bean for each year of your age.

events.title: Gion Matsuri: the mikoshi leave
events.verb: Watch the mikoshi lifted at the steps
events.text: On the evening of 17 July, after the float procession, the shrine's three mikoshi gather at the foot of its west steps at 18:00 and set out for a week in the town.
lines: Six o'clock, at the foot of the stone steps. Three gilded mikoshi, hundreds of men in white, and one shout: hoitto, hoitto. All three are lifted to arm's length at once.
The floats of the morning were to clear the way for this. The kami ride out to their resting place on Shijo and come home on the 24th.

events.title: Okera-mairi
events.verb: Light a rope at the okera fire
events.text: On New Year's Eve, people light a bamboo rope at the shrine's okera fire and carry it home, swinging it to keep it alight.
lines: Iron lanterns burn with okera root, a bitter medicinal herb, and everyone holds out a length of rope to catch the fire.
Then you walk home swinging the rope in small circles so that it stays alight, and cook the year's first meal on it. All down Shijo, little red circles in the dark.
